e01.abstract.existence.TorusEuler.theorem11: The theorem produces one smooth odd datum and a maximal solution with a positive finite lifespan. Its equations have no external force, and its periodic fields on $\mathbb R^3$ represent fields on the torus. Diverging central vorticity prevents smooth continuation even though the velocity stays bounded.

e01.abstract.central-vorticity.TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness: The witness requires $|\operatorname{curl}u(t,0)|\to\infty$ as $t\uparrow T_*$. Oddness makes $u(t,0)=0$, so the vorticity growth is measured along a single stationary particle. The limit requires all sufficiently late times to exceed each fixed magnitude.

e01.abstract.bounded-velocity.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S678b.closedSlab_ve: The stage velocity increments are summable in supremum norm, yielding one continuous limit on the whole closed time slab. The theorem identifies that uniform limit with the classical Euler velocity before the singular time. The stronger spatial Hölder convergence in the abstract uses additional bounds.

e01.abstract.off-origin.TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness: The witness applies the off-origin limit condition separately to $u$ and $\partial_tu$. Every spatial derivative through order $m$ converges uniformly on compact sets that avoid the lattice points. The lattice is how the single removed point of the torus appears in the periodic lift.
e01.abstract.off-origin.TorusEuler.HasOffOriginLimits: The definition takes one field at a time. For each compact set away from the lattice and each $m$, it asks for a local $C^m$ limit and uniform convergence of the derivatives through order $m$. The witness uses that condition for both fields named in the abstract.

e01.torus.cell.TorusEuler.centeredCell: The formal cube has one coordinate interval $[-1/2,1/2]$ in each of the three directions. Periodic fields identify opposite faces by integer translation. The cube itself is the domain used to integrate one period of a lifted field.

e01.euler-equations.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution: The definition writes the transport term as $D_xu(t,x)u(t,x)$. It requires momentum balance with zero forcing and zero divergence for each $0\le t<T_*$ in the periodic lift. At time zero the derivative is from the right. The lifespan and vorticity conclusions use further results.

r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.theorem_1_1: `EulerSingularityWitness` packages all the assertions in the printed theorem for one datum $u_0$, time $T_*$ and solution $u,p$. The last quantifier then ranges over any maximal solution from that same datum and requires equality of its lifespan and its velocity on $[0,T_*)$. That quantifier spells out the classical uniqueness used in the paper.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_1_1: The numbered Lean theorem provides one smooth odd datum and one maximal periodic solution for every part of the passage. The common endpoint $T_*$ governs both divergent integrals, the bounded-speed and central-curl pair, and the spatial limits of $u$ and $\partial_tu$. It also proves equality of lifespan and velocity for any other maximal solution from the chosen datum.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.IsMaximalEulerSolution: `IsMaximalEulerSolution` first requires a smooth periodic Euler solution on $[0,T_*)$. It then rules out a smooth Euler solution on every longer interval whose velocity agrees with $u$ throughout $[0,T_*)$. The existence and uniqueness assertions in Theorem 1.1 use this definition as a condition on a candidate solution.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution.velocity_eq_o: Give the theorem two smooth periodic Euler solutions with the same initial velocity. It proves that their velocities agree for every $0\le t<\min(T_1,T_2)$, the interval on which both are defined. Theorem 1.1 combines this agreement with maximality to compare their lifespans.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.EulerSingularityWitness: `EulerSingularityWitness` groups the hypotheses and conclusions about the chosen $u_0,T_*,u,p$. Joint smoothness is part of being a maximal classical solution, and $u(t,-x)=-u(t,x)$ is a separate clause. For that same $u$ it requires both infinite time integrals, a single speed bound, central curl tending to infinity, and off-origin spatial limits for $u$ and $\partial_tu$.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution: `IsEulerSolution` takes $T_*$ to be a real number and requires $T_*>0$. This gives a positive finite endpoint whenever the condition holds. The remaining fields require the Euler equations and joint smoothness on the half-open interval, with periodic velocity and mean-zero periodic pressure.
r5-root-theorem11-complete.TorusEuler.HasOffOriginLimits: `HasOffOriginLimits` translates the compact-set clause into a statement about a supplied field on the periodic lift. For each $K$ avoiding $\mathbb Z^3$ and each $m$, there is a local $C^m$ limit on a neighborhood of $K$, and convergence on $K$ is uniform for every spatial derivative up to order $m$. The main witness separately supplies the condition for $u$ and for $\partial_tu$.

adapted.E1-03.3.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.remark_1_2: The same solution whose vorticity diverges at the origin has a smooth velocity extension across the terminal time at every other point of the torus. Remark 1.2 asserts smoothness in time as well as space there. The extension after $T_*$ carries no Euler equation.

r2a1.intro.wave.background.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: The trace is zero so $Dx$ preserves the divergence condition, and symmetry of $D'+D^2$ lets its acceleration come from a quadratic pressure. The theorem retains both requirements and needs a time derivative of $D$ on the interval. The wave and profile hypotheses supply the rest of the Euler identity.

r2a1.intro.wave.velocity.TorusEuler.affineWaveVelocity: The velocity definition adds the oscillation $\mathbf a(t)F(k(t)\cdot x)$ to $D(t)x$, so the displayed $w$ is its second term. The perpendicularity written beside $w$ is a wave hypothesis used in the Euler proof and is independent of the velocity definition.
r2a1.intro.wave.velocity.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: The exact-wave theorem takes the transverse profile in the display as part of its hypotheses. With the wave ODE and an admissible affine background it verifies Euler for the sum $Dx+w$. Perpendicularity removes the wave's divergence and self-advection during that verification.

adapted.E1-05.1.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_1: At fixed time $k$ is the normal to every plane of constant phase. The oscillatory part of the velocity is a scalar multiple of $\mathbf a$, so the perpendicularity $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$ in Lemma 2.1 makes it tangent. The full velocity includes the separate background $Dx$.

intro.origin-gradient.TorusEuler.hasFDerivAt_planeWave: The spatial chain rule gives the derivative at any $x$ as $F'(k\cdot x)\,\mathbf a\otimes k$. The passage uses $x=0$ and unit slope there. The theorem concerns a spatial derivative of the wave profile, independent of its evolution in time.

intro.self-advection.TorusEuler.planeWave_selfAdvection: The derivative of $w=\mathbf aF(k\cdot x)$ in the direction $w$ has a factor $k\cdot\mathbf a$. The formal theorem uses that factor to make self-advection vanish at each point where the phase profile is differentiable.

r2a1.intro.phase-and-pressure-cancellati.TorusEuler.affineWave_materialAccelerati: With the phase transported by $Dx$, the material acceleration reduces to $(D'+D^2)x+(\mathbf a'+D\mathbf a)F(k\cdot x)$. The formula uses transversality to remove self-advection. The amplitude ODE then supplies the coefficient needed to cancel the wave pressure.
r2a1.intro.phase-and-pressure-cancellati.TorusEuler.hasGradientAt_affineWavePress: Differentiating the quadratic pressure gives $-Sx$ by symmetry. Differentiating the wave primitive gives $-p_{\rm w}F(k\cdot x)k$. Choosing $S=D'+D^2$ and using the amplitude ODE makes these terms cancel the two pieces of the material acceleration.

intro.affine-equations.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.WaveOn: On a specified time interval $J$, the formal condition requires $k_t=-D^Tk$ and $\mathbf a_t=-D\mathbf a+2(k\cdot D\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$ at every time in $J$. These are exactly the displayed evolution equations with the coefficient substituted. Derivatives are taken within $J$, hence one-sided at included endpoints. The condition alone imposes neither $k\ne0$ nor $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$; those are separate wave hypotheses. Its quotient is assigned zero at $k=0$, a case excluded in the introductory wave.
intro.affine-equations.TorusEuler.affineWavePressureCoeff: The paper displays two differential equations and the pressure coefficient. This formal definition supplies only $p_{\rm w}=2k\cdot D\mathbf a/|k|^2$; it does not assert either evolution equation. The quotient is assigned zero at $k=0$, whereas the introductory wave has $k\ne0$.

intro.pressure-transversality.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_affineWavePa: Under the wave equations the pairing derivative is $-2k\cdot D\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}|k|^2$. Setting it to zero with $k\ne0$ gives the coefficient in (1.4). The formal theorem checks the zero derivative using that chosen coefficient, so zero initial pairing is preserved when applied along the interval.

intro.affine-pressure.TorusEuler.affineWavePressure: The pressure definition adds $-p_{\rm w}P(k\cdot x)$ to the background quadratic pressure. Because $P'=F$, taking the gradient of this wave term gives $-p_{\rm w}F(k\cdot x)k$, the direction and sign needed in the amplitude equation.

intro.affine-euler.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: The exact-wave theorem verifies the unforced equations for $Dx+w$ on $\mathbb R^3$. The wave-vector ODE transports the phase, the amplitude ODE supplies the pressure cancellation, and transversality gives zero wave divergence. The formal identity only requires a differentiable profile with the given primitive.

intro-amplification-new-frame.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame: The formal frame normalizes the wave normal and amplitude and takes their cross product for the third vector. Their nonzero lengths and perpendicularity give an orthonormal frame. Expressing the older gradient in that frame produces the two couplings used for the next wave.

intro-amplification-new-couplings.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry: The entry definition takes the component along $E_i$ of the map applied to $E_j$. With the new frame, choose $j=2$ in both cases, then $i=1$ for $\nu_+$ and $i=3$ for $\eta_+$. Their positivity is part of the amplification argument.

adapted.E1-08.1.TorusEuler.localizedCurl_properties: The transported vector potential is already zero near the faces where periodic copies meet. Taking its curl commutes with integer translation and preserves that vanishing, which is why the wave remains smooth across the faces even when the phase itself is not periodic.
adapted.E1-08.1.TorusEuler.initialLocalizedCompletedWave: At activation the radial cutoff gives the vector potential support inside the cell. Its curl is smooth and periodic across the seams, so the phase $k\cdot x$ may have an arbitrary nonzero real normal, subject to the perpendicularity of the starting amplitude.

e01.initial-shear.euler.TorusEuler.isEulerSolution_stationaryShe: The starting flow is stationary and has no velocity component in the direction $e_2$ in which it varies. Its divergence and self-advection therefore vanish, so zero pressure solves Euler. The formal result allows any real $\rho$ on a positive lifespan.

e01.initial-shear.formula.TorusEuler.stationaryShear: The definition is evaluated on $\mathbb R^3$ using the three coordinate vectors. Its sine factor is unchanged by integer translations and reverses sign under $x\mapsto-x$, which gives the periodic odd field used as the parent.

e01.initial-shear.couplings.TorusEuler.stationaryShearGradient_origi: Differentiating the sine at zero gives the factor $2\pi$. The derivative sends $v$ to $2\pi v_2(e_1+\rho e_3)$. Applying the two coordinate projections to this map gives the couplings, whose numerical readout is a separate theorem.
e01.initial-shear.couplings.TorusEuler.stationaryShearGradient_coupl: The formal coupling identity reads two entries of the central shear map. The $e_1$ component of its value on $e_2$ is $2\pi$ and the $e_3$ component is $2\pi\rho$. This gives the values in the passage after identifying the map with $\nabla U_0(0)$.

e01.endpoint.first-variation-equation.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_endpointDisp: Differentiate $\xi=Fz$ with $F_t=MF$ and $z_t=v$. This gives $\xi_t=M\xi+Fv$, where $Fv=b\circ X$ in (1.5). The initial displacement comes from the fixed labels, so at time zero this equation reads $\xi_t(0,a)=b(0,a)$.
e01.endpoint.first-variation-equation.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution: The mean-solution definition uses label displacement $z$ and its velocity $v$. Setting $\xi=(D_aX)z$ and multiplying out its time derivative gives (1.5), since the second term is $(D_aX)v=b\circ X$. Both endpoint conditions fall on $z$, leaving the initial velocity free to be selected.

adapted.E1-10.1.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_4_2: The endpoint problem has two zero displacement conditions. Theorem 4.2 solves for the label velocity and the constant field $c$ at the same time. At time zero, where the flow derivative is the identity, $c$ is the divergence-free initial velocity that gives zero final displacement.

e01.endpoint.linearized-euler.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse_smooth_for: The theorem solves (1.6) for a smooth periodic force under flow and quadratic-form bounds on the parent, with the two displacement endpoints fixed. For the first mean the passage chooses $f$ to be the negative phase-averaged wave error and parent residual. The inverse works with this force even when the parent does not solve Euler exactly.

adapted.E1-11.1.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_4_1: Test the inequality on a vector at any fixed time and label. Lemma 4.1 integrates it along a displacement $\xi$ that vanishes at both ends, where the time Poincaré estimate bounds $\int|\xi|^2$ by a fraction of $\int|\xi_t|^2$. This gives the lower bound on the label energy.

e01.endpoint.pressure-cancellation.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.det_labelDeriva: The change of variables $x=X(t,a)$ has Jacobian determinant one for the divergence-free parent. Thus the label integral of the pressure pairing becomes the unweighted torus integral against the physical displacement, where the separate divergence identity applies.
e01.endpoint.pressure-cancellation.TorusEuler.integral_inner_gradient_cente: Periodic integration by parts gives $\int_{\mathbb T^3}\nabla q\cdot w=0$ for a divergence-free $w$. In the passage $w=\xi\circ X^{-1}$ is the displacement in physical coordinates. Volume preservation supplies the change of variables before applying the integral identity.

e01.endpoint.coercivity.TorusEuler.endpointDisplacementEnergy_co: For a single path ending at zero, write $\xi(t)=-\int_t^T\xi_\tau\,d\tau$ and use Cauchy–Schwarz. This bounds the adverse contribution to the energy by $T^2/2$ times the derivative norm because $H\le I$. Integrating over labels and using $T\le1$ gives the displayed version.
e01.endpoint.coercivity.TorusEuler.endpointLabelEnergy_coercive: The theorem proves the half-kinetic lower bound in the label variables, using $\xi=Fz$ with zero endpoint values of $z$. The skew term in the label energy accounts for the moving frame. The estimate applies with a one-sided upper bound on $H^\#$, so a large negative direction is allowed.

adapted.E1-13.1.TorusEuler.endpointHessian_eq_pressureHe: Differentiating the momentum residual in space gives $D_xR_U=M_t+M^2+D_x^2p_U$ along $X$. Moving the first two terms to the other side gives the effective Hessian $H^\#$. The residual derivative therefore matters even when the residual itself is small.

The general Hessian has a term $-cF_h'(	heta)

abla	heta$. For constant $c=p_{m w}$ and a linear phase, the latter terms vanish. The surviving rank-one term has zero eigenvalues in both directions tangent to the phase planes.

localized.intro.profile-slopes.TorusEuler.hasDerivAt_waveProfile_zero: The normalization result supplies the equality $F_h'(0)=1$ in (1.10). The wave gradient at zero phase is therefore $\mathbf a\otimes k$ even as $h$ shrinks. The slope bounds away from zero come from the other declaration.
localized.intro.profile-slopes.TorusEuler.deriv_waveProfile_bounds: The theorem supplies the inequalities in (1.10) for every phase, with $C=1/2$. Because the pressure curvature uses the negative of the slope, the lower bound is the one that constrains positive curvature. The upper bound still permits the large negative curvature at the center.

adapted.E1-13.3.TorusEuler.hasDerivAt_waveProfile_zero: When the phase at the origin is zero, differentiating $\mathbf a F_h(k\cdot x)$ gives $F_h'(0)\,\mathbf a\otimes k$. The scalar derivative theorem fixes that multiplier at one, so narrowing the profile leaves the central shear unchanged.

adapted.E1-13.4.TorusEuler.deriv_waveProfile_bounds: The associated pressure Hessian is $-p_{\rm w}F_h' k\otimes k$. For $p_{\rm w}>0$ its only possible positive eigenvalue is in the normal direction where $F_h'<0$. The bound $F_h'\ge-h/2$ limits that part while allowing unit slope at the center.

localized.intro.positive-curvature.TorusEuler.wavePrimaryPressure_leading_u: For nonnegative $p_{\rm w}$, the negative part of $F_h'$ is the only source of positive normal curvature in this rank-one term. The formula in the theorem bounds its quadratic form above by $(h/2)p_{\rm w}|k|^2$ times the squared length of the test vector.

adapted.E1-13.8.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_3_1: A periodic primitive needs a slope of integral zero. In the construction for Lemma 3.1, subtract the mean from a narrow periodic bump and divide by the resulting value at zero. The negative slope is shallow because the bump occupies only a portion of width $O(h)$.

adapted.E1-13.5.TorusEuler.norm_waveProfile_le: The estimate $|F_h(s)|\le h/2$ holds at every phase. Multiplying by $|\mathbf a|$ gives the wave's velocity bound at once. This small velocity follows from the profile height, while the shear at the center uses its unit slope.

adapted.E1-14.1.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_B_1: A spatial derivative of a retained Fourier mode contributes a factor of its wave number. Lemma B.1 turns this into a supremum norm estimate for the smooth cutoff, so controlling the retained frequency band bounds each fixed higher derivative of the parent.

localized.intro.phase-trajectory.TorusEuler.transportedProfile_on_traject: The transport identity says that evaluating a profile along $x=X(t,a)$ restores the original label and its phase $k_*\cdot a$. Choosing the profile to return its phase gives the first equality. The normal $\nabla_x\theta$ is defined by a spatial derivative of that carried phase.

adapted.E1-14.2.TorusEuler.hasGradientAt_transportedPhas: Differentiate $\theta(t,X(t,a))=k_*\cdot a$ in $a$ at fixed $t$. The resulting equation is $(D_aX)^T\kappa=k_*$, so the old normal is multiplied by the inverse transpose of the deformation. This gradient identity allows a stationary normal as well as a turning one.

localized.intro.time-cutoff.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff: The cutoff definition requires smoothness on the stage, values in $[0,1]$, and zero before the chosen activation time. Those conditions impose inactivity in the earlier interval. The later rise to one is supplied by a particular choice of cutoff.
localized.intro.time-cutoff.TorusEuler.PaperWaveCutoff.first: The first-wave cutoff is the constant function one, with activation time zero. Its time derivative vanishes, so no activation residual comes from that cutoff. Later waves use separate cutoffs that vary in time.

localized.intro.level-profile.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Zd: The definition makes $Z_p$ the sum of the current oscillation, its mean, and the completion carried over from the preceding oscillation. The last completion has index $P+1$, so the separate finite-sum identity places it beyond the last $Z_p$ in the display.
localized.intro.level-profile.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.Cd: The stored completion is indexed by the oscillation that generates it. The definition of the paper's $C_p$ reads the completion of $V_{p-1}$ at positive indices. That index shift explains why the last generated correction appears beyond the summed $Z_p$ levels.
localized.intro.level-profile.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.expansion: The expansion sums $V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p$ through $P$. In that convention each completion sits beside the oscillation that generates it. Reindexing with $C_1=0$ gives the displayed form, leaving $C_{P+1}$ as the extra term.
localized.intro.level-profile.TorusEuler.HierarchyProfiles.velocity_eq: The equality reindexes the sum of completions by one. The assumed $C_1=0$ contributes nothing at the start, so rewriting the summands as $Z_p$ leaves $C_{P+1}$ outside the sum. This is a finite identity of profile sums.

adapted.E1-15.1.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_5_6: Theorem 5.6 supplies a finite expansion in which the completion of $V_p$ appears as $C_{p+1}$, including the completion of the last oscillation. Transversality removes the phase derivative in the divergence of $V_p$. Adding the curl correction removes the remaining slow divergence.

localized.intro.phase-split.TorusEuler.phaseMean: The definition integrates the profile over $0\le s\le1$ while keeping the other inputs fixed. With input $H_2$ it gives the mean source's phase-average term. The oscillatory difference is obtained separately by subtracting this integral.
localized.intro.phase-split.TorusEuler.phaseOscillation: The definition removes the constant-in-phase part by subtracting the integral over the unit period. Integrating the resulting profile again gives zero for an integrable input. With input $H_2$, this is the forcing component used for the oscillatory solve.

e01.correction.mean-source.TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.level_two_: At level two the phase-average identity retains the additional term $-R_U$ after computing the averaged wave interactions. In the mean equation it gives the response the sign required to cancel the old momentum residual along with the new average.
e01.correction.mean-source.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.meanSource: The mean source is defined to include $-R_U\circ X$ when $p=2$. The other levels use just the negative average of $H_p$. This assigns cancellation of the old residual to the first mean equation, where the residual is expressed in particle labels.

e01.correction.mean-equation.TorusEuler.paper_mean_inverse_smooth_for: Use the forcing $f=-\langle H_2\rangle_s-R_U$ in the linearized equation for the mean. The endpoint inverse supplies a smooth divergence-free velocity and a pressure gradient for such a smooth force under the flow and quadratic-form bounds. It chooses the initial value through the zero final displacement condition.
e01.correction.mean-equation.TorusEuler.HierarchyOperators.level_two_: The phase average at level two separates into an averaged slow advection term and the mean contribution of the curl completion. The source identity puts both on the right with a minus sign and includes $-R_U$. This produces the particular forcing for the mean equation once the phase-average identities hold.

e01.correction.mean-endpoints.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution: The label displacement is $z$, with physical displacement $\xi=(D_aX)z$. Requiring $z(0)=z(T)=0$ in the solution definition makes $\xi$ vanish at both endpoints. Existence for that constraint comes from the endpoint inverse.
e01.correction.mean-endpoints.TorusEuler.PaperSmoothMeanSolution.mean_: For the same forcing and admissible parent, any two smooth solutions with zero displacement at both endpoints have the same mean velocity $B_2$. This forces their initial values to agree as well. The inverse's existence result supplies the solution whose initial value is selected.

localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.FiniteHierarchySolvers.constr: The formal theorem organizes the mean and oscillatory equations for every retained level $2\le p\le P$, assuming their linear solvers and prescribed operations. At $p=2$ its source has the algebraic form in (1.12). It does not itself identify the abstract operations with physical derivatives or assert $\kappa\cdot V_2=0$ and $\langle V_2\rangle_s=0$. Those geometric constraints come from the supplied transverse solutions.
localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.exists_oscillatoryPhaseSolve_: For continuous coefficients along a single particle label, a transported initially nonzero covector and a continuous period-one zero-mean force, the formal theorem constructs a zero-initial periodic transverse solution with normalized phase pressure. It proves the differential equation at each phase. It does not insert the particular source containing $H_2,B_2$, or prove its smooth dependence on labels, as required for the displayed spatial field.
localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.TransverseSolution: The formal definition requires $V_t+MV+\kappa\partial_s\pi=f$, transversality, zero phase mean and zero initial data, with normalized phase pressure. It therefore specifies the left side and constraints of (1.12) for a general source. It neither identifies the particular right side nor proves existence of such a solution.
localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsExpansion: An admissible expansion requires the transverse equation with its oscillatory and supplementary sources, with $V_1=\widetilde\chi A_1$ and $C_1=0$. At level two these sources give exactly (1.12), and the transverse-solution condition includes perpendicularity, zero phase mean and zero initial data. This is part of the definition of an admissible finite expansion; its existence is a separate theorem.
localized.intro.transverse-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.suppSource: The formal definition supplies only the supplementary forcing $-\sum_{i=2}^p(B_i\cdot\kappa)\partial_sY_{p+1-i}$. At $p=2$, $Y_1=V_1$ because $C_1=0$, so it becomes $-(B_2\cdot\kappa)\partial_s(\widetilde\chi A_1)$. The remaining source, differential equation and transverse constraints are not conclusions of this definition.

localized.intro.mean-fast-zero-average.TorusEuler.hierarchy_phaseMean_supplemen: At fixed time and position, $(B_2\cdot\kappa)$ is constant in $s$. The integral of $\partial_sV_1$ over one period is $V_1(1)-V_1(0)=0$. The formal identity applies this cancellation to the extra advection source.

adapted.E1-15A.1.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_5_3: For each label and phase, Lemma 5.3 constructs the zero-start transverse response to a smooth forcing of the required parity and phase mean. The pressure term is along $\kappa$, so its role in the ODE is to keep the evolving velocity in the plane perpendicular to $\kappa$.

adapted.E1-15A.2.TorusEuler.slowFastDivergence_curlComple: The curl construction gives a profile whose slow divergence plus its phase contribution to divergence is zero. After substituting $s=\theta(t,x)$, the chain rule makes this sum the physical divergence. For the second oscillation the two terms of that completed profile are $V_2$ and $C_3$.

localized.intro.next-level-completion.TorusEuler.hierarchy_completion_previous: The formal theorem gives the correction exponent from level $p-1$ as the oscillatory exponent at level $p$ minus $1/3$. At $p=3$, this explains why the correction of $V_2$ fits into level three. It is an equality between powers assigned to estimates. It does not prove an estimate for $C_3$ or construct the next mean and oscillatory solutions.

adapted.E1-15A.3.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.TransverseSolution: In the definition, $V(0,a,s)=0$ is a condition for every particle label and phase, imposed alongside the forced equation and transverse constraint. It concerns the correction's initial velocity. The mean correction uses a separate displacement condition.

e01.correction.retained-completion.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.expansion: In the definition $\sum_{p=1}^P(V_p+C_{p+1}+B_p)$, the last summand contains both $V_P$ and its completion $C_{P+1}$. Stopping the level sum therefore retains the term needed to make the last oscillation divergence free.
e01.correction.retained-completion.TorusEuler.Paper.S5.IsExpansion: The expansion conditions impose $C_{p+1}=C[V_p]$ through $p=P$ and set the next oscillation and mean to zero. That leaves the final curl completion in place when passing to the finite expansion used in the iteration.
e01.correction.retained-completion.TorusEuler.HierarchyProfiles.velocity: The sum stores a completion at the index of the oscillation that generates it. Thus the entry indexed by $P$ already contains the paper's $C_{P+1}$. This declaration defines the finite velocity perturbation before the parent is added and the phase is evaluated.

adapted.E1-15.2.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_5_6: The oscillatory estimates in Theorem 5.6 carry a power $\lambda^{-5/4-2(p-1)/3}$ at level $p$. Raising $p$ by one supplies the factor $\lambda^{-2/3}$ in the passage. The derivative bounds still have level-dependent constants and factors controlled by the parent.

e01.correction.cutoff-error.TorusEuler.paperProposition511_physicalC: The child velocity is obtained by a smooth Fourier multiplier at scale $\Lambda$. For $P>2$ the factor $\Lambda^{2-P}$ in the velocity difference decays with the cutoff frequency at fixed $C^{P,1/2}$ size. The theorem also estimates the resulting changes in residual and pressure Hessian.

e01.correction.transported-support.TorusEuler.HierarchyTwistedProfile.Physi: At a physical point $x$, the theorem checks the inverse-flow label $X^{-1}(t,x)$. The oscillatory increment is zero if that label lies outside the chosen support, and it also vanishes before activation. Shrinking support in the labels and bounds on the parent flow then give the shrinking physical neighborhoods before Fourier truncation.

r5-ind-figure4-inactive.TorusEuler.Paper.Theorem71Conclusions.os: The vanishing field of the construction's conclusion requires $O_i=0$ before and at $t_i$ for each later wave. This is the thick segment in the figure. It concerns the oscillatory increment, while the mean correction is governed by its own equations.

r5-ind-figure4-crossing.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerConstruction.ce: The central-waves record has a crossing condition at the activation time of the next stage. Thus the marked point is where the prescribed ratio for the present wave is reached and the next wave launches. The record refers to a selected crossing.

r5-ind-figure4-endpoint.TorusEuler.Paper.theorem_7_1: The theorem gives a common finite limit $T_\infty$ of the launch times, strictly below every stage's endpoint $S_i$. Each approximate velocity remains smooth on its own closed interval $[0,S_i]$. The limit can therefore be studied up to $T_\infty$ using every stage.

e01.conventions.leray-projection.TorusEuler.periodicL2Coefficient_sub_rea: The paper writes the spatial identity $\mathbb P=I-\nabla\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}$. The formal theorem proves its equality of Fourier coefficients for real $L^2$ vector fields on the unit torus. The inverse Laplacian’s constant mode is zero, so constant velocity modes are retained. The coefficient identity is the Fourier formulation of the projection, rather than a pointwise classical identity for arbitrary fields.
e01.conventions.leray-projection.TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode: For a frequency $k\in\mathbb Z^3$ and vector coefficient $a$, the formal definition gives only the scalar multiplier $-2\pi i(k\cdot a)/(4\pi^2|k|^2)$ when $k\ne0$, with value zero at $k=0$. This is the scalar part $\Delta^{-1}\operatorname{div}$ of the paper’s projection formula. It neither constructs a spatial field nor states the full projection identity.
e01.conventions.leray-projection.TorusEuler.pressureCorrectionMode_zero: The formal theorem proves that the scalar correction’s zero Fourier coefficient vanishes, fixing the mean of the potential. The paper additionally gives the full identity for the Leray projection. The single zero-mode statement does not establish that identity and does not remove the constant part of velocity.

e01.conventions.pressure-normalization.TorusEuler.IsEulerSolution: The momentum equation depends on $\nabla p$, so adding a function of time to $p$ would preserve the equation. The exact-solution definition chooses the representative with zero integral over the volume-one torus at every time. The adapted sentence extends the same convention to approximate Poisson pressures.

e01.conventions.periodic-flow-displaceme.TorusEuler.IsLabelFlowOn.add_latticeVect: The flow of a periodic uniformly Lipschitz velocity carries $x+n$ to the trajectory of $x$ translated by $n$. Subtracting the starting position removes this extra integer vector, so the displacement is a periodic field on the torus.

r2a1.intro.derivative-conventions.TorusEuler.divergence: The linked definition takes the trace of the derivative of a vector field, giving $\sum_i\partial_i v_i$ when the derivative exists. Applying that operation to each row gives the rowwise convention in the passage. The declaration itself is for vector fields.

r5-root-schedule-purpose.TorusEuler.paperTheorem71: The construction uses a schedule to obtain smooth stages with an oscillation and a correction both bounded by $\lambda_j^{-1}$ in their respective norms, the latter through $q_j$. Increasing $q_j$ gives eventual control of any fixed derivative order. Summability also needs the growth of the selected frequencies.
r5-root-schedule-purpose.TorusEuler.PaperTheorem71Conclusions: The conclusion record demands the estimates the schedule must deliver, including an oscillation of size at most $\lambda_j^{-1}$ and a correction controlled through $q_j$. It describes those bounds for a supplied sequence. Choosing frequencies and proving that the construction meets the bounds take separate results.

e01.parameters.log-floor.TorusEuler.fixedOrderThreshold_log_floor: For the explicitly chosen threshold, the formal theorem gives $\log\mathcal B(s)\ge4K(s+1)^3$ for every nonnegative integer $s$ and $b$. The paper uses $s\ge1$ and $b\ge1$. Positivity follows from the exponential term in that particular threshold, so no extension convention for the logarithm is involved.
e01.parameters.log-floor.TorusEuler.Paper.AdmissibleThreshold: The admissibility condition imposes exactly the floor (1.13) at every positive integer $s$, with a separate requirement $\mathcal B(s)>0$. It records a hypothesis on the chosen threshold. It does not prove that an arbitrary function satisfies it.

e01.parameters.schedule.TorusEuler.frequencySchedule_exists: The formal theorem constructs $q_j,\lambda_j$ satisfying $q_1=1$, $\lambda_0=N$, the frequency recurrence and the maximum rule, assuming $b\ge1$, $N\ge1$ and $\mathcal B(1)\le N$. It does not define $\Lambda_j,L_j,\varepsilon_j$ or prove their bounds. These are separate parts of the displayed schedule.
e01.parameters.schedule.TorusEuler.InductiveEulerParameters: The formal parameter conditions record $q_1=1$, the recurrence and maximum rule, positivity and the logarithmic threshold floor. They do not contain the entire display: the cutoff frequencies, logarithmic gains and coupling ratios are defined elsewhere. They also omit threshold monotonicity and cost domination, and assert no existence by themselves.
e01.parameters.schedule.TorusEuler.Paper.Schedule.L: This formal definition gives exactly $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$ for a supplied real frequency sequence. It defines only the gain part of (1.14), not the recurrence or maximum rule. Under the paper’s frequencies $\lambda_j>1$, the gains are positive.
e01.parameters.schedule.TorusEuler.Paper.Schedule.ε: This formal definition gives $\varepsilon_j=L_{j+1}^{-2}$, which is (1.14) after shifting the index. It also assigns a value at the unused index zero and assigns zero if the gain is zero. The paper uses positive gains and $j\ge1$. The other parts of the schedule are not stated here.

e01.lemma13.orders.TorusEuler.paperLemma13_slowOrders: As the preceding frequency grows, an order already admitted by its threshold stays available for the next maximum. The cap on that maximum allows an increase of at most one. When the frequencies tend to infinity, every fixed order eventually becomes attainable.
e01.lemma13.orders.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_1_3: The hypothesis written `IsGreatest` selects the largest order whose threshold fits the preceding frequency and whose value is at most $q_j+1$. The conclusion bounds the change at each step and separately gives divergence of the whole order sequence.
e01.lemma13.orders.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_1_3: The named theorem gives a single schedule two properties used in the later construction. Consecutive allowed orders differ by at most one, and each fixed derivative order is eventually allowed. The finite step estimates and the limiting smoothness argument use those properties at different points.
e01.lemma13.orders.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_1_3: The proof calls the schedule theorem with index $i=j-1$ to turn the paper's first positive stage into $i=0$. It takes the successive-order inequalities from that theorem at index $i$ and reuses convergence of the same full order sequence directly.

e01.lemma13.logarithmic-bound.TorusEuler.paperLemma13_slowOrders: The later logarithm equals the earlier logarithm times three successive frequency exponents. The threshold floor was chosen to dominate four times that product even if the order rises at both intervening steps. Multiplying by the earlier logarithm gives the square on the right.
e01.lemma13.logarithmic-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_1_3: Here `Schedule.L freq (j + 1)` is $4\log\lambda_{j+2}$. The last clause states the comparison with $\log^2\lambda_{j-1}$ for every positive $j$. The paper uses this to pay for a coming wave's gain using a preceding frequency.
e01.lemma13.logarithmic-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_1_3: The numbered theorem packages the logarithmic bound in the paper's stage indices. It is available to later stage estimates as $L_{j+1}\le(\log\lambda_{j-1})^2$, so any fixed power of this gain can eventually be absorbed by a positive power of the preceding frequency.
e01.lemma13.logarithmic-bound.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_1_3: In the last proof branch, take $j=i+1$ and unfold `Schedule.L`. This turns the desired left side into four times the logarithm of `freq (i + 3)` and the right side into the square of the logarithm of `freq i`. The core log bound then applies directly.

affine.background-hypotheses.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: In the affine-wave assertion the trace clause controls divergence of the background and the symmetry clause allows cancellation by the gradient of $-\tfrac12 x\cdot(D'+D^2)x$. The theorem also needs the wave ODE and transversality. Smooth $D$ is included under its time derivative assumption.
affine.background-hypotheses.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_1: The statement of Lemma 2.1 makes trace zero and symmetry explicit. Trace zero is the divergence condition for $Dx$, and symmetry lets the acceleration matrix be written as the gradient of a quadratic potential. The formal statement uses time differentiability of $D$ on an interval with unique relative derivatives.

affine.wave-equations.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.WaveOn: The formal condition includes $k'=-D^Tk$ and $\mathbf a'=-D\mathbf a+2(k\cdot D\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$, but not the last relation $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$ in (2.1). That missing transversality condition is supplied separately to the Euler theorem.
affine.wave-equations.TorusEuler.affineWavePressureCoeff: The definition gives only the coefficient $p_{\rm w}=2k\cdot D\mathbf a/|k|^2$ from the four displayed relations. It does not assert either evolution equation or $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$, and at $k=0$ its quotient is assigned zero.
affine.wave-equations.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: The formal statement assumes the two wave equations and, for its Euler conclusion, perpendicularity. Its conclusions are the Euler equations and persistence of nonzero transverse data. It does not assert that arbitrary supplied paths satisfy (2.1).
affine.wave-equations.TorusEuler.Paper.WaveOn: The formal condition states the two wave equations with the displayed pressure coefficient but omits $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$. Thus it expresses only the first three relations of (2.1). The fourth must be assumed independently.

affine.euler-and-pressure.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: The formal statement proves zero divergence and the Euler momentum equation on $\mathbb R^3$ with exactly the displayed pressure. It requires only differentiable $F$, $P'=F$ and a differentiable trace-free $D$ with symmetric $D'+D^2$, rather than the paper’s smooth odd periodic normalized profile. It also allows $k=0$ in this part, with division by zero assigned zero; nonzero data are required separately for persistence.
affine.euler-and-pressure.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_1: The formal statement proves zero divergence and the Euler momentum equation on $\mathbb R^3$ with exactly the displayed pressure. It requires only differentiable $F$, $P'=F$ and a differentiable trace-free $D$ with symmetric $D'+D^2$, rather than the paper’s smooth odd periodic normalized profile. It also allows $k=0$ in this part, with division by zero assigned zero; nonzero data are required separately for persistence.
affine.euler-and-pressure.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_1: The formal statement proves zero divergence and the Euler momentum equation on $\mathbb R^3$ with exactly the displayed pressure. It requires only differentiable $F$, $P'=F$ and a differentiable trace-free $D$ with symmetric $D'+D^2$, rather than the paper’s smooth odd periodic normalized profile. It also allows $k=0$ in this part, with division by zero assigned zero; nonzero data are required separately for persistence.

affine.nonzero-perpendicular.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.exactWave: Nonzero perpendicular data at any $t_0\in J$ remain so throughout $J$, including earlier times. The paper states nonzero perpendicularity for $t\ge t_0$ in the interval of existence. The formal statement gives the same properties for every $t$ in the same interval, including $t<t_0$, assuming the wave equations, initial nonzero perpendicular data, and the stated background regularity. It makes no claim outside that interval.
affine.nonzero-perpendicular.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_1: Nonzero perpendicular data at any $t_0\in J$ remain so throughout $J$, including earlier times. The paper states nonzero perpendicularity for $t\ge t_0$ in the interval of existence. The formal statement gives the same properties for every $t$ in the same interval, including $t<t_0$, assuming the wave equations, initial nonzero perpendicular data, and the stated background regularity. It makes no claim outside that interval.

r2a1.wave.phase-transport.TorusEuler.affineWave_materialAccelerati: The paper separately asserts transport of $k\cdot x$ and of $w$ by $Dx$. The formal acceleration identity uses $k'=-D^Tk$ and gives their combined consequence for $u=Dx+w$, namely $(D'+D^2)x+(\mathbf a'+D\mathbf a)F$. It does not conclude either of the two displayed transport identities by itself.

r2a1.wave.self-advection.TorusEuler.planeWave_selfAdvection: Under $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$ and differentiability of $F$ at $k\cdot x$, the formal statement proves the final equality $(w\cdot\nabla)w=0$. It does not separately state the displayed intermediate expression $(k\cdot\mathbf a)FF'\mathbf a$, although that calculation is used in its proof.

r2a1.wave.acceleration.TorusEuler.affineWave_materialAccelerati: The acceleration identity agrees exactly, with only differentiability at the evaluated phase and time required. Unlike the standing hypotheses of Lemma 2.1, this calculation does not need the amplitude equation, zero trace or symmetry of $D'+D^2$; it assumes phase transport $k'=-D^Tk$ and transversality.

r2a1.wave.pressure-gradient.TorusEuler.hasGradientAt_affineWavePress: The formal statement gives $\nabla p=-Sx-p_{\rm w}F(k\cdot x)k$ under symmetry of $S$ and $P'=F$ at the phase. Taking $S=D'+D^2$ gives the pressure terms in the paper. Identifying the second acceleration term with $p_{\rm w}kF$ still requires the amplitude equation, which is not a hypothesis or conclusion of this spatial-gradient identity.

r2a1.wave.divergence.TorusEuler.divergence_affineWaveVelocity: The formal statement proves $\operatorname{div}u=\operatorname{tr}D+(k\cdot\mathbf a)F'$ for a profile differentiable at the phase. The paper also concludes zero. That final equality requires the additional substitutions $\operatorname{tr}D=0$ and $k\cdot\mathbf a=0$, which this identity does not assume.

affine.pairing-cancellation.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_affineWavePa: For an arbitrary coefficient $p_{\rm w}$, the formal statement proves only $(k\cdot\mathbf a)'=-2k\cdot D\mathbf a+p_{\rm w}|k|^2$. It does not assert the final zero in the paper. That requires the chosen pressure coefficient and cancellation of the nonzero denominator.

For $k\ne0$ and the two wave equations with $p_{\rm w}=2k\cdot D\mathbf a/|k|^2$, the formal statement proves $(k\cdot\mathbf a)'=0$. It states the final cancellation, not the intermediate equality for an arbitrary pressure coefficient. The two linked statements supply the two parts of the displayed calculation.

affine.wave-vector-nonvanishing.TorusEuler.linearODE_ne_zero_of_mem: Take the operator in the linear ODE to be $-D(t)^T$. If the wave vector were zero at any time, uniqueness with that zero value would force the solution to be zero also at $t_0$. The theorem applies to continuous bounded-linear coefficients on the interval.

affine.linear-amplitude-equation.TorusEuler.affineWaveAmplitudeOperator: The paper states an evolution equation. The formal definition gives its linear right-hand-side operator $\mathbf a\mapsto-D\mathbf a+2(k\cdot D\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$, equivalent to the displayed projection formula when $k\ne0$. It does not assert that any path has this derivative. The wave-equation condition supplies that assumption. At $k=0$ the operator is defined as $-D$.

affine.amplitude-nonvanishing.TorusEuler.linearODE_ne_zero_of_mem: Once the wave vector stays nonzero, the factor $1/|k(t)|^2$ in the amplitude equation is continuous. The right-hand side is then a continuous linear operator applied to $\mathbf a$. The theorem uses uniqueness at a hypothetical zero to show that a nonzero initial amplitude stays nonzero.

adapted.E1-16.1.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_1: At fixed time the derivative of the phase in the wave's own direction is $\mathbf a\cdot k$. Consequently the self-advection term contains a factor $\mathbf a\cdot k=0$. Lemma 2.1 uses this cancellation in verifying Euler for the sum of the wave and its affine background.

c8-frame-trace-scope.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_2: For nonzero transverse solutions of the wave equations, the formal statement assumes $\operatorname{tr}B=0$ and no symmetry of $B'+B^2$. In fact it does not require a time derivative of $B$ at all. The supplied derivatives of $k$ and $\mathbf a$ suffice for the frame calculation.

frame.normalized-axes.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.frame: The formal triple is exactly $(k/|k|,\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|,(k/|k|)\times(\mathbf a/|\mathbf a|))$. On the paper’s nonzero perpendicular data it is an orthonormal frame. The definition also accepts zero vectors, normalizing them to zero; those extra values do not describe the paper’s wave frame.

frame.matrix-entries.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.entry: The formal entry is the Euclidean scalar product $E_i\cdot BE_j$. Its first, second and third positions correspond to the paper’s indices $1,2,3$. Orthonormality is not imposed by the definition. It is supplied by the wave-frame hypotheses when these scalar products are read as matrix entries.

frame.strength-couplings.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_movingFrame: The formal frame identity uses $\nu=E_1\cdot BE_2$, $\eta=E_3\cdot BE_2$ and the logarithm of $|k||\mathbf a|$, so the three quantities agree with the paper. Nonzero perpendicular data justify the normalized axes and make the strength positive.

frame.derivative-identities.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.movingFrameDeriva: The formal statement gives all four identities in (2.2), and explicitly proves orthonormality. It assumes nonzero perpendicular wave data and zero trace, with derivatives relative to the time set, but does not require the smoothness of $B$ assumed in the paper. No symmetry of $B'+B^2$ is needed.
frame.derivative-identities.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_2: The formal statement gives all four identities in (2.2), and explicitly proves orthonormality. It assumes nonzero perpendicular wave data and zero trace, with derivatives relative to the time set, but does not require the smoothness of $B$ assumed in the paper. No symmetry of $B'+B^2$ is needed.
frame.derivative-identities.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_2: The formal statement gives all four identities in (2.2), and explicitly proves orthonormality. It assumes nonzero perpendicular wave data and zero trace, with derivatives relative to the time set, but does not require the smoothness of $B$ assumed in the paper. No symmetry of $B'+B^2$ is needed.

r2a1.wave.normalized-vector.TorusEuler.normalizeDerivOfScaled: The paper displays both the unit-vector and logarithmic-norm derivatives. This formal statement gives the first: when $v\ne0$ and $v'=|v|w$, it proves $(v/|v|)'=w-((v/|v|)\cdot w)(v/|v|)$. Taking $w=v'/|v|$ gives the paper’s formula. The logarithmic derivative is supplied by the other link.
r2a1.wave.normalized-vector.TorusEuler.logNormDerivOfScaled: This formal statement supplies the second displayed identity: for $v\ne0$ and $v'=|v|w$, it gives $(\log|v|)'=(v/|v|)\cdot w$. It does not state the unit-vector derivative. Both statements permit any real inner-product space and relative time derivatives.

r2a1.wave.first-axis.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_movingFrame: The formal frame statement proves $E_1'=-B_{12}E_2-B_{13}E_3$ under nonzero perpendicular wave data and zero trace. It does not separately conclude the projection formula or $(\log|k|)'=-B_{11}$ shown here; its logarithmic conclusion concerns $|k||\mathbf a|$.
r2a1.wave.first-axis.TorusEuler.logNormDerivOfScaled: The formal statement gives $(\log|v|)'=(v/|v|)\cdot(v'/|v|)$ for a nonzero differentiable vector. To obtain the paper’s $(\log|k|)'=-B_{11}$, one substitutes $v=k$ and $k'=-B^Tk$. The first-axis equation is a separate linked conclusion.

r2a1.wave.second-axis.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_movingFrame: The formal frame statement gives $E_2'=B_{12}E_1-B_{32}E_3$ from the nonzero transverse wave equations and zero trace. It does not separately state the displayed projection formula or $(\log|\mathbf a|)'=-B_{22}$; its scalar conclusion is the derivative of the logarithm of the product.
r2a1.wave.second-axis.TorusEuler.logNormDerivOfScaled: For a nonzero differentiable vector $v$, the formal statement gives $(\log|v|)'=(v/|v|)\cdot(v'/|v|)$. Substituting the transverse amplitude equation cancels the pressure term and gives $(\log|\mathbf a|)'=-B_{22}$. It is the general derivative rule needed for this equality, not its specialized wave conclusion.

r2a1.wave.cross-axis.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_movingFrame: The formal statement gives the final identity $E_3'=B_{13}E_1+B_{32}E_2$ for the nonzero transverse wave frame over trace-free $B$. The displayed product rule $E_3'=E_1'\times E_2+E_1\times E_2'$ occurs in the proof, not as a separate conclusion of this declaration.

frame.log-strength-calculation.TorusEuler.hasDerivWithinAt_movingFrame: The formal statement concludes $(\log(|k||\mathbf a|))'=B_{33}$ under zero trace. The paper also displays its decomposition as $-B_{11}-B_{22}$; that intermediate equality is used in the proof but is not stated as a separate conclusion here.

r5-reference-reference-system-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_3: In the constant-entry model, the statement first gives equations for the scaled finite-shear vector and matrix. It then specifies uniform convergence of the amplitude coefficient matrix to the reference matrix for fixed $\varepsilon$ and interval length. The large parameter being sent to infinity is the shear.
r5-reference-reference-system-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_3: Lemma 2.3 proves the reference system by keeping the two entries fixed in the moving frame and taking the strong-shear limit of the scaled coefficient matrix. The convergence is uniform on the prescribed normalized interval. Lemma 2.4 separately allows the entries to drift at finite shear.

r5-reference-additive-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_4: The statement of Lemma 2.4 makes the finite shear comparison quantitative through an error matrix bounded by $CT^p\delta$. The same matrix works for all transverse amplitudes on the chosen interval. A solution comparison needs Lemma 2.6 to estimate the effect of that error over time.
r5-reference-additive-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_4: The proved lemma controls the scaled wave vector and the change in the two-dimensional amplitude equation under the prescribed smallness assumptions. This gives the coefficient comparison used in the passage. Dividing by the growing reference solution is the next step in comparing actual amplitudes.

r5-reference-relative-comparison-overvie.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_6: The formal bound keeps $\alpha_1/\alpha_2$ close to $-Y$, the ratio of the reference solution's two scaled components. That ratio records direction independently of overall amplitude. The error bound needs the stated smallness of $C_0T^{C_0}\delta$ on the fixed interval.
r5-reference-relative-comparison-overvie.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_6: Lemma 2.6 proves that after normalization the wave direction stays close to the reference direction, with error polynomial in $T$ times the coefficient error. It also bounds $\log(|\mathbf a|/a_{\rm ref})$. The interval and smallness conditions are required for both estimates.

r5-reference-crossing-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.proposition_2: The proposition's statement defines shear at the crossing as the product of the amplitude and wave-number length. It bounds that product relative to $\lambda$ times the peak amplitude, and bounds the early amplitude relative to that same peak. Both estimates use the normalized clock.
r5-reference-crossing-overview.TorusEuler.Paper.proposition_2_8: The proof bounds shear at each crossing in its prescribed late interval by constant multiples of $\lambda\max|\mathbf a|/\sqrt{\varepsilon\varepsilon_+}$. It also proves that on the first normalized time unit the amplitude is at most $e^{3-\varepsilon^{-1/2}}\max|\mathbf a|$. The early bound keeps the wave small while its own cutoff rises.

additive.prescribed-wave-data.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl: The paper assumes a smooth trace-free older gradient and nonzero transverse preceding wave. The formal data require only continuous $B$ and $E_c$ on a compact physical time set, and include the same preceding wave equations and nonzero perpendicularity there. They also include positive activation couplings $B_{12}(t_0),B_{32}(t_0)$, which the paper imposes in the following paragraph. This records assumptions rather than proving existence of such data.

r2a1.wave.gradient.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl: The formal definition gives $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$, the first expression in the display. It does not by itself state the equality $\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p=\sigma_pE_2\otimes E_1$; that normalized-tensor identity is supplied by the other linked statement.
r2a1.wave.gradient.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r: The formal identity proves $(\sigma/r)(\sigma_p/\sigma)E_2\otimes E_1=(\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p)/r$, assuming nonzero preceding vectors at the base and evaluated times and $r\ne0$. It identifies the shear term after division by $r$; multiplying by $r$ and adding $B+E_c$ recovers the paper’s full decomposition. The base time is zero in this identity and must be shifted to $t_0$.

r2a1.wave.new-vector.TorusEuler.Paper.NewWaveVector: The formal condition requires $\lambda>0$, $k(t_0)=\lambda E_3(t_0)$ and $k'=-M^Tk$ throughout the compact physical time set $I$, where $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$ and $E_3$ is the preceding wave’s third unit direction. This is exactly the mathematical condition stated in the quoted sentence.

r2a1.wave.amplitude.TorusEuler.Paper.AmplitudeVector: For a prescribed wave vector $k$ on a compact physical time set $I$, the formal condition requires $\mathbf a'=-M\mathbf a+2(k\cdot M\mathbf a)k/|k|^2$ and $\mathbf a\cdot k=0$ at every time in $I$, where $M=B+\mathbf a_p\otimes k_p+E_c$. This is exactly the mathematical condition stated in the quoted sentence.

r2a1.wave.frozen-couplings.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl: The product is the size of the rank-one shear contribution when $k_p$ and $\mathbf a_p$ are perpendicular. This formal definition gives only $\sigma=|k_p(t_0)||\mathbf a_p(t_0)|$. The displayed definitions and positivity of $\nu$ and $\eta$ belong to the other links.
This formal definition gives only $\nu=E_1(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)$. The positivity $\nu>0$ is an assumption in the supplied physical data. The strength and second coupling are separate definitions.

This formal definition gives only $\eta=E_3(t_0)\cdot B(t_0)E_2(t_0)$. Positivity is part of the physical data, rather than a conclusion of this formula, and the other displayed quantities are defined separately.

The formal data assume positive $B_{12}(t_0)$ and $B_{32}(t_0)$ and nonzero preceding vectors, making all three frozen quantities positive. They do not themselves give the three displayed naming equations; those are the separate linked definitions.

additive.time-scales.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.PhysicalAmpl: This definition supplies $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$ with positive activation strength and first coupling. The other three scales and the time relation in the display are separate definitions.
This definition supplies $S=\sigma/r$. With $r=\sqrt{2\sigma\nu}$ and positive $\sigma,\nu$, it equals the paper’s square root. It does not by itself define $r$, $\varepsilon$ or $\tau$.
This definition supplies only $\varepsilon=\eta/\nu$, with positive activation couplings. It imposes no additional smallness condition. The rate, shear scale and time relation are separate.

The paper defines normalized time by $\tau=r(t-t_0)$. The formal clock gives its inverse, $t=t_0+\tau/r$. Since the amplification data have $r>0$, the two relations are equivalent. The clock definition does not include the other displayed scale identities.

r2a1.wave.scaled-pair.TorusEuler.Paper.zeta: The formal vector consists of the projections $(E_1\cdot k,S E_2\cdot k,E_3\cdot k)/\lambda$ at $t=t_0+\tau/r$. For an orthonormal frame and $\lambda>0$, these are exactly the wave-vector coordinates in (2.3). This definition does not give the amplitude expansion.
r2a1.wave.scaled-pair.TorusEuler.Paper.alpha: The formal vector is $(S E_1\cdot\mathbf a,E_2\cdot\mathbf a,S E_3\cdot\mathbf a)$ at $t=t_0+\tau/r$, which gives the amplitude part of (2.3) in the orthonormal frame. It does not define the wave-vector coordinates or impose the amplitude equation.
r2a1.wave.scaled-pair.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.scaled_waveV: The formal statement proves only the first expansion in (2.3), for an orthonormal frame and nonzero $\lambda,S$. It reconstructs $k$ from its scaled projections. The amplitude expansion is not a conclusion.
r2a1.wave.scaled-pair.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.U: The paper’s first amplitude coordinate is $\alpha_1=S E_1\cdot\mathbf a$. This formal coordinate is $-\alpha_1$. It supplies only that signed component, so the intermediate system must be conjugated by $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)$ before its signs are compared with the paper.
r2a1.wave.scaled-pair.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.V: This formal coordinate is $E_2\cdot\mathbf a=\alpha_2$, with no scaling by $S$. It gives only the second amplitude component of the two displayed expansions.

r2a1.wave.initial-coordinates.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.coordinate_i: The paper obtains $\zeta(0)=(0,0,1)$ for the launched wave. The formal identity only requires an orthonormal frame at $t_0$, nonzero $\lambda$ and $k(t_0)=\lambda E_3(t_0)$; neither $\lambda>0$ nor the wave equation nor positive $S$ is needed. Its base time is $t_0$, corresponding to $\tau=0$.

r2a1.wave.norm-factor.TorusEuler.Paper.scaledNormSq: The formal definition gives $m=\zeta_1^2+\zeta_2^2/S^2+\zeta_3^2$, but does not state $|k|^2=\lambda^2m$. That equality additionally uses the scaled coordinates and orthonormal frame. At $S=0$, the definition assigns zero to its middle quotient.
r2a1.wave.norm-factor.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.wave_norm_sq_: For an orthonormal frame and nonzero $\lambda,S$, the formal identity proves exactly $|k|^2=\lambda^2m$ with the displayed $m$. It is pointwise algebra and requires no wave equation.

r2a1.wave.third-coordinate.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.amplitude_dec: The formal statement reconstructs the whole transverse amplitude from the pair $(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ in an orthonormal frame, with $\lambda,S,\zeta_3\ne0$. Its third physical projection is $(\zeta_1(-\alpha_1)-\zeta_2\alpha_2)/(S\zeta_3)$. Multiplying by $S$ gives exactly the paper’s formula for $\alpha_3$.

r2a1.wave.reference-angle.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle: The formal definition selects $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$ for all real inputs. It fixes the branch but does not itself assert the displayed range or define $\zeta_0$; those are the other linked statements.
r2a1.wave.reference-angle.TorusEuler.Paper.zetaRef: `zetaRef` builds the reference vector with coordinates $(\tan\varphi,-\varepsilon\tau,1)$, where $\varphi$ is the arctangent of $\varepsilon\tau^2/2$. The linked tangent and range lemmas justify the substitution for its first coordinate and the branch of the angle in (2.4).
r2a1.wave.reference-angle.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceAngle_mem: For $\varepsilon\ge0$, the argument $\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ of the arctangent is nonnegative, and $0\le\varphi<\pi/2$. The theorem supplies the branch condition in (2.4), in particular the positive cosine used for the reference wave.
r2a1.wave.reference-angle.TorusEuler.Paper.tan_referenceAngle: Applying tangent cancels the arctangent in the definition of $\varphi$, giving $\tan\varphi=\varepsilon\tau^2/2$ for every real $\varepsilon,\tau$. This is the substitution for the first component of the reference vector. The range lemma supplies the separate nonnegativity condition on the angle.
r2a1.wave.reference-angle.TorusEuler.ReferenceRiccati.x: This formal scalar is $\varepsilon\tau^2/2$, the first coordinate of the reference vector after using the tangent identity. It does not define the angle, prove its range or define the other two coordinates.

adapted.E1-17.2.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_3: The reference scaled vector still has second component $-\varepsilon\tau$. Undoing the scaling divides that component by $S$, which tends to infinity with the preceding shear. The two unscaled components then give the stated limit in the moving frame.

adapted.E1-17.1.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_4: Lemma 2.4 compares the scaled vector $\zeta$ at a finite shear with the explicit reference $\zeta_0$. The estimate is in scaled components, with an error bounded in terms of the comparison length and the coefficient error $\delta$. The physical component in the $E_2$ direction can be nonzero.

r2a1.wave.model-hypotheses.TorusEuler.Paper.ModelCase: In the moving frame, the model gradient sends the second basis vector to $\nu E_1+\eta E_3$ and sends the other two to zero. The definition also sets the central error to zero on the window. These are the model inputs from which the wave-vector equations are derived.
r2a1.wave.model-hypotheses.TorusEuler.Paper.modelEntries: The formal matrix lists the two potentially nonzero entries $B_{12}=\nu$, $B_{32}=\eta$. By itself it neither requires an actual background to have these entries throughout $[0,T]$ nor states $E_c=0$. Those time-dependent requirements belong to the linked model condition.

r2a1.wave.constant-model-strength.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_3: Under the two-entry model, launched wave and active-interval hypotheses, the formal statement concludes $|k_p(t)||\mathbf a_p(t)|=\sigma$ throughout the normalized interval, exactly the quoted constant strength.
r2a1.wave.constant-model-strength.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_3: The formal statement proves the constant-strength conclusion under the model assumptions, as one part of the full Lemma 2.3. No constancy of the older gradient in fixed spatial coordinates is required.

r2a1.wave.model-vector-equations.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_3: The three formal derivatives are the displayed equations for $\zeta$ in normalized time, under the model and launch assumptions. At $0,T$ they are derivatives taken from within $[0,T]$.
r2a1.wave.model-vector-equations.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.model_case_equa: The formal calculation gives exactly these three equations and does not need $T\ge2$, but it assumes the full frame theorem of Lemma 2.2 as an input. Thus it records the derivation of this part of Lemma 2.3 from a prior result. The final numbered theorem supplies that prior proof.

r2a1.wave.model-amplitude-equations.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_3: For every transverse amplitude, the formal statement gives exactly the two displayed derivatives wherever $\zeta_3\ne0$, with the same $\Pi$ and weighted denominator $m$. The standing model hypotheses ensure $S>0$.
r2a1.wave.model-amplitude-equations.TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearPressure: The formal definition supplies only the displayed rational expression for $\Pi$. It does not assert the amplitude equations. At a zero denominator it assigns zero. The model application uses $\zeta_3\ne0$, which makes $m>0$.
r2a1.wave.model-amplitude-equations.TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearMatrix: The formal definition expands the displayed right-hand sides into a matrix acting on $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$. It neither states that an amplitude has this derivative nor imposes $\zeta_3\ne0$; that differential-equation assertion is supplied by the model theorem.
r2a1.wave.model-amplitude-equations.TorusEuler.Paper.strongShearMatrix_mulVe: The formal identity proves that matrix multiplication gives exactly these two right-hand sides, including $\Pi$. It does not state the derivatives on the left or the existence of an amplitude solution. The differential equations require the separate model-wave hypotheses.

r2a1.wave.uniform-strong-shear-limit.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_3: The formal statement uses one threshold $S_0(\varepsilon,T,e)$ for every model configuration and every $\tau\in[0,T]$, bounding the Euclidean wave-vector error and each matrix-entry error by $e$. It additionally guarantees $\zeta_3\ne0$ beyond that threshold, and allows continuous background data on a compact physical set containing the active interval.
r2a1.wave.uniform-strong-shear-limit.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.strongShear_lim: The formal statement gives the same uniform estimates and nonzero third coordinate, but assumes the frame theorem of Lemma 2.2 as a hypothesis. The threshold is chosen before the physical configuration and time. This is the conditional construction of the limit. The final numbered Lemma 2.3 supplies the frame theorem.

r2a1.wave.reference-system.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceSystemMatrix: The formal definition gives exactly the coefficient matrix of (2.5) in $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$. It does not assert that a supplied amplitude solves the displayed differential equations. That is additional solution data.
r2a1.wave.reference-system.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.referenceMatr: The formal matrix acts on $(-\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$, with both off-diagonal signs opposite to (2.5). Conjugating by $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)$ gives the paper’s matrix. This definition supplies coefficients, not a solution or a differential-equation conclusion.
r2a1.wave.reference-system.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.referenceSystem: The formal identity identifies the four entries of the paper-coordinate reference matrix as the negative damping coefficient, negative driving coefficient, $-1$ and $0$. It does not state that an amplitude satisfies the differential equation or prove convergence from finite shear.

r2a1.wave.frame-gives-model-strength.TorusEuler.Paper.Proof.lemma_2_3_of: This formal statement assumes Lemma 2.2 and deduces all of Lemma 2.3, including constant preceding strength. It does not separately state the three specialized physical frame derivatives or the intervening derivative of $\log\sigma_p$; those are steps of the proof.
r2a1.wave.frame-gives-model-strength.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.model_case_equa: The formal calculation concludes $\sigma_p=\sigma$ and the scaled wave and amplitude equations, conditional on the frame theorem. The quoted three physical frame derivatives and the equality $(\log\sigma_p)'=0$ are used in the calculation but are not separate conclusions of this declaration.
r2a1.wave.frame-gives-model-strength.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_2: Lemma 2.2 gives the general frame derivatives and $(\log\sigma_p)'=B_{33}$ for a nonzero transverse wave. Substituting the two-entry model gives the displayed derivatives and zero logarithmic derivative. Constancy of $\sigma_p$ still requires the interval argument and its activation value, not stated by this link.

r2a1.wave.physical-model-vector.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.model_case_equa: The formal conclusion gives the scaled equations for $\zeta$ in $\tau$, conditional on the frame theorem and model hypotheses. The paper displays equations for $k_i=k\cdot E_i$ in physical time $t$. Using $k_1=\lambda\zeta_1$, $k_2=\lambda\zeta_2/S$, $k_3=\lambda\zeta_3$ and $d\tau/dt=r$ recovers the quoted equations; they are not separately stated conclusions here.

r2a1.wave.physical-model-amplitude.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.model_case_equa: The formal conclusion gives the reduced equations for $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ in normalized time, assuming $\zeta_3\ne0$ and the frame theorem. The paper displays physical components $a_i=\mathbf a\cdot E_i$ and the pressure coefficient. Recovering these formulas requires $a_1=\alpha_1/S$, $a_2=\alpha_2$, elimination of $a_3$ by transversality, and reversal of the time rescaling.

r2a1.wave.scale-identities.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.nu_div_rate:
The formal identity is $
u/r=1/(2S)$ for positive activation data. It gives $
u S/r=1/2$ after multiplication by $S$, and helps obtain $
u/\sigma=1/(2S^2)$. It does not itself state the full five-identity display.
r2a1.wave.scale-identities.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.eta_div_rate: The formal identity is $\eta/r=\varepsilon/(2S)$ for positive activation data. Multiplication by $S$ gives $\eta S/r=\varepsilon/2$; the additional identity for $\eta/\sigma$ uses $rS=\sigma$. The other displayed equations are not conclusions here.
r2a1.wave.scale-identities.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.rate_sq: The formal statement proves $r^2=2\sigma\nu$. The paper’s display instead lists consequences involving $S=\sigma/r$ and $\varepsilon=\eta/\nu$. The positive scale definitions are needed to derive those identities. This single square identity is not the whole display.

r2a1.wave.gronwall-limit.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.zeta_bounds: For $\mu=1/(2S^2)\in[0,1]$ and $\varepsilon\ge0$, the formal statement bounds each coordinate error by $\mu K(\varepsilon,T)$, with $K=\varepsilon T(1+\varepsilon)(e^{(2+\varepsilon)T}-1)/(2+\varepsilon)$. For fixed $\varepsilon,T$ this quantitative bound implies the paper’s uniform convergence. It assumes the exact model differential equations and initial data.
r2a1.wave.gronwall-limit.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.strongShear_lim: The formal statement gives uniform convergence of the wave vector and amplitude coefficients for every model configuration, conditional on Lemma 2.2. It asserts the resulting limit and eventual $\zeta_3\ne0$, rather than the paper’s description of Gronwall’s argument. The preceding quantitative declaration supplies that estimate.

r2a1.wave.coefficient-limits.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.strongShear_lim: The formal statement controls all four coefficient differences uniformly in time, giving the two displayed limits as part of that conclusion. It assumes the frame theorem, model equations, launch data and sufficiently large shear. The paper’s intermediate trigonometric equalities are identified by the other link.
r2a1.wave.coefficient-limits.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.referenceSystem: The formal identity evaluates the limiting coefficient expressions at $(\zeta,S^{-2})=(\varepsilon\tau^2/2,-\varepsilon\tau,1,0)$ and obtains the reference matrix. It identifies the limits in the display, but contains no assertion that the actual coefficients converge to them.

c8-reference-system-name.TorusEuler.Paper.referenceSystemMatrix: This coefficient matrix is what the paper calls the reference system. The definition by itself asserts no differential equation for a supplied function.

c8-reference-vector-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.zetaRef: The formal definition gives the explicit function $\zeta_0=(\varepsilon\tau^2/2,-\varepsilon\tau,1)$ but does not state its derivative. Differentiating those components gives the paper’s triangular system. The formula alone is not a differential-equation theorem.
c8-reference-vector-equation.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2a.zeta_bounds: The formal statement assumes a solution of the perturbed model system and bounds its difference from this explicit reference function. At zero perturbation it identifies any such solution with the reference vector, but it does not construct that solution or separately state the reference vector’s derivatives.

r2a1.wave.physical-error.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio: The definition sums two relative coupling drifts and two ratios for the background and the gradient error. Its suprema are in physical time, so taking the image of $[0,T]$ under the clock gives exactly the comparisons in (2.6). The finite-shear estimate uses that single error to control longer normalized intervals.

adapted.E1-18.1.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_4: The first two terms of the error $\delta$ measure the departures of the actual frame entries from the launch values $\nu$ and $\eta$. Lemma 2.4 uses them together with the other background and shear errors to bound the difference between the actual and reference systems on the prescribed interval.

additive.finite-smallness.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.additiveCompariso: The formal statement uses precisely these two inequalities as assumptions, with $C_0$ a nonnegative integer above an absolute threshold $N\ge240$. Its conclusion is the wave-vector and amplitude comparison. It is not a definition or proof that (2.7) holds for arbitrary data.
additive.finite-smallness.TorusEuler.Paper.FiniteSmallness: The formal condition is exactly the two displayed inequalities, with $C_0$ a nonnegative integer and $T^{C_0}$ an integer power. The sufficiently large threshold for $C_0$ and $T\ge2$ are imposed by the theorems using it, not by the condition itself.

r2a1.wave.strong-shear-bounds.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.normalized_r: The formal statement gives $S^{-1}\le2\delta$ and normalized gradient bounds, under compactness, continuous data and positive activation values. It does not state the displayed chain through $C_0^2T^{C_0}/2$ or the bound $S^{-2}\le\delta$; these require additional scalar consequences of (2.7).
r2a1.wave.strong-shear-bounds.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.amplificatio: Under $T\ge2$, nonnegative $\varepsilon,\delta$, positive $S$, $S^{-1}\le2\delta$ and (2.7) with integer $C_0\ge240$, the formal statement proves $S\ge T^2$ along with other smallness bounds. It does not state the intermediate lower bound in $C_0$ or $S^{-2}\le\delta$, and its sufficient threshold is larger than the paper’s $C_0\ge2$ for this calculation.

r5-waves-parameter-ratio.TorusEuler.Paper.Schedule.ε: The formal schedule defines $\varepsilon_j=L_{j+1}^{-2}$, with $L_j=4\log\lambda_{j+1}$. For $j\ge1$ this is the ratio prescribed by (1.14), written there as $\varepsilon_{j-1}=L_j^{-2}$ for $j\ge2$. This definition alone does not prove the paragraph’s additional bounds on $\varepsilon^{-1}$, $T$ or $\delta$; those belong to the later application of the schedule.

r2a1.wave.coefficient-list.TorusEuler.MovingAmplitude.scaledAmplitu: The paper lists thirteen scalar quantities for the case $E_c=0$, including $S^{-2}$. The formal input list includes all scaled entries of both the older and full gradients, the three wave-vector coordinates and the reciprocals $S^{-1},\zeta_3^{-1},m^{-1}$. Specializing the full gradient and forming products yields the paper’s coefficients, but the lists are not literally the same.

r2a1.wave.vector-comparison.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_4: The formal statement proves both displayed bounds, with an absolute real factor $C$ and a separate nonnegative integer exponent $p$ in $CT^p\delta$. These are chosen before the sufficiently large integer $C_0$ and all wave data. It allows continuous $B$ on a larger compact physical observation set, using that set’s suprema for $\delta$, and additionally supplies a continuous common amplitude-error matrix and the preceding-strength bound.
r2a1.wave.vector-comparison.TorusEuler.Paper.lemma_2_4: The formal statement proves both displayed bounds, with an absolute real factor $C$ and a separate nonnegative integer exponent $p$ in $CT^p\delta$. These are chosen before the sufficiently large integer $C_0$ and all wave data. It allows continuous $B$ on a larger compact physical observation set, using that set’s suprema for $\delta$, and additionally supplies a continuous common amplitude-error matrix and the preceding-strength bound.
r2a1.wave.vector-comparison.TorusEuler.PaperAffine.additiveCompariso: The formal statement proves the Euclidean and summed coordinate error from $\zeta_0$ bounded by $CT^p\delta\le1/2$. It does not include the relative error in $|k|^2\cos^2\varphi/\lambda^2$, which is the second half of (2.10). That estimate is added in the full numbered lemma.

r2a1.wave.safe-coordinates.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_4: With $\zeta=(k\cdot E_1,Sk\cdot E_2,k\cdot E_3)/\lambda$ and $\varphi=\arctan(\varepsilon\tau^2/2)$, the formal statement gives $|\zeta-(\tan\varphi,-\varepsilon\tau,1)|$, $||k|^2\cos^2\varphi/\lambda^2-1|\le CT^p\delta\le1/2$, $1/2\le\zeta_3\le3/2$, $|\zeta|\le3T^2$, and $|\sigma_p/\sigma-1|\le2T\delta$. Under the complete amplification hypotheses and (2.7), the formal statement gives both bounds in (2.11), with Euclidean $|\zeta|$.
r2a1.wave.safe-coordinates.TorusEuler.MovingWaveVector.waveVector_c: Assuming a summed coordinate error at most $1/2$, the formal statement gives $1/2\le\zeta_3\le3/2$, $|\zeta_1|\le T^2$, $|\zeta_2|\le T$, and $m\ge1/4$. It does not directly state the Euclidean bound $|\zeta|\le3T^2$; that follows by combining the coordinate bounds.
r2a1.wave.safe-coordinates.TorusEuler.Paper.Lib.S2b.norm_zeta_le: The formal statement proves only $|\zeta|\le3T^2$, assuming the three coordinate bounds, including $1/2\le\zeta_3\le3/2$. It does not establish the latter bounds or derive them from the physical smallness condition.

r2a1.wave.amplitude-comparison-system.TorusEuler.Paper.Statement.lemma_2_4: The formal statement gives the displayed equation with one continuous $\mathcal E$ chosen before every amplitude, and $\|\mathcal E\|\le CT^p\delta$.
